chapter_intro: Jeremiah’s Struggles with God and Judah.

passages.title: Jeremiah’s Struggles with God and Judah.
passages.text: As the nation faces invasion, Jeremiah struggles to serve God faithfully. He is surprised by opposition (11:1–12:17), stunned over feeling betrayed by God (13:1–15:21), renewed by God (16:1–17:18), burdened by opposition (17:19–18:23), and prepared to continue serving (19:1–20:18).

notes.text: Judah has four places to go: plague (pestilence), battle (sword), starvation (famine), and exile (captivity).

make them a horror. They will serve as a reminder of God’s wrath for all nations (Deut. 28:25). Manasseh ruled Judah c. 697–642 b.c. He committed idolatry, practiced child sacrifice, used fortune-tellers, and generally led Judah to hate God’s word (2 Chron. 33:1–9). He repented late in life (2 Chron. 33:10–20).
Who? Judah has no allies, and God has left them.
relenting. God is weary of holding back punishment. The people do not change their ways despite the mercy he shows when he relents.
The primary reason for punishment was that they did not turn from their ways.
She who bore seven. A mother with the perfect number of sons losing all she has represents Judah’s reversal of fortunes.
Judah’s sins have brought her to the edge of financial ruin and exile.
you know. God has seen Jeremiah’s suffering. take me not away. Jeremiah asks to be spared when death strikes.
Your words were found, and I ate them. As a true prophet, Jeremiah digested, delighted in, and spoke God’s words in God’s name for the people’s good.
a deceitful brook. Jeremiah accuses God of failing to protect him.
If you utter what is precious. God rebukes Jeremiah, urging repentance and faithful, truthful speech about himself. Jeremiah must side with God, not with the people.
God repeats his promise to protect (1:17–19). God will deliver Jeremiah, but the promise implies continued persecution.
